blocks.text: D. Do you want to make a wager and leave it to Lamachus (to say) which taste better, locusts or thrushes? L. Alas! how unjust you are. D. He prefers the locusts. And [III, 330] there the Scholiast says: Διασύρει τὸν Λάμαχον, ὡς ἀκρίδας ἐσθίοντα, ἢ ὅτι πρότερον εὐτελεῖ ἐχρῆτο τῇ διαίτῃ [Diasyrei ton Lamachon, hōs akridas esthionta, ē hoti proteron euteleī echrēto tē diaitē]; he mocks Lamachus as one who feeds on locusts, or because he had formerly used cheap food. Plutarch, in the Banquet, says that a tyrant who would rather rule over slaves than over men is like a farmer who would want ἀκρίδας, καὶ ὀρνίθας, ἀντὶ πυρῶν, καὶ κριθῶν συγκομίζειν [akridas, kai ornithas, anti pyrōn, kai krithōn synkomizein], to gather locusts and birds instead of wheat and barley (to eat). In Theophylact's Letters a certain rustic, boasting that he had been lavishly entertained, says: Ἰσχάδες, ἦν μοι, καὶ ἀκρίδες, τὰ ὄψα· ὁ δὲ θεσπέσιος οὑτοσὶ νεανίας τῶν ἰσχάδων τὰ πλεῖστα ἐκβέβρωκε καὶ τὰς ἀκρίδας, οὐκ οἶδ᾽ ὅπως, ἐξερροφήσει [Ischades, ēn moi, kai akrides, ta opsa; ho de thespesios houtosi neanias tōn ischadōn ta pleista ekbebrōke kai tas akridas, ouk oid᾽ hopōs, exerrophēsei]. I had, he says, dried figs and locusts as a relish; but that divine young man devoured most of the figs, and the locusts too, I know not how, he gulped down. [col. 491] So too Athenaeus, book 4, testifies that the ancients used to eat little creatures very like locusts, namely cicadas and cercopes, which are smaller cicadas, and indeed to whet the appetite. His words are: Ἤσθιον δὲ καὶ τέττιγας, καὶ κέρκωπας, ἀναστομώσεως χάριν [Ēsthion de kai tettigas, kai kerkōpas, anastomōseōs charin]. In the same place Anaxandrides, describing the preparations for the wedding of Iphicrates, when he took to wife the daughter of Cotys, king of Thrace, lists among other things τέττιγας ὀπτοὺς [tettigas optous], cooked cicadas. And from the Anagyrus of Aristophanes this is quoted: Πρὸς Θεῶν ἐρᾷς τέττιγα φαγεῖν, καὶ κερκώπην θηρευσαμένη καλάμῳ λεπτῷ [Pros Theōn eras tettiga phagein, kai kerkōpēn thēreusamenē kalamō leptō]. By the gods, you gladly eat the cicada and the cercope, which you hunt with a thin reed. And in book 9, Aristophanes in the Horae praises Athens because even in winter the huckster sells there κίκλας, ἀπίους, σχαδόνας, ἐλάας, πύον, χόρια, χελιδόνα, τέττιγας [kiklas, apious, schadonas, elaas, pyon, choria, chelidona, tettigas], thrushes, pears, honeycombs, olives, beestings, choria (that is, dishes made of milk and honey), swallows, cicadas. Likewise in book 2 Alexis brings on an old woman whose usual food, as she herself says, is κύαμος, θέρμος, λάχανον, γογγυλὶς, ὦχρος, λάθυρος, φηγὸς, βόλβος, τέττιξ [kyamos, thermos, lachanon, gongylis, ōchros, lathyros, phēgos, bolbos, tettix], the bean, the lupine, greens, the turnip, the bitter vetch, the chickling, the acorn of the oak, the bulb, the cicada. Indeed the Philosopher, History book 5, ch. 30, and after him Pliny, book 11, ch. 26, teach at what season above all they taste best. And Pliny testifies that peoples in the East eat them, among them the Parthians, although abounding in wealth. Hence Aelian, History book 10, ch. 6, is greatly indignant at the men of his age, some of whom sell the cicadas, an animal sacred to the Muses, strung in a row, for dinner, while others buy them and eat them greedily.

But, and this is the heart of the matter, the locust was edible among the Jews too. This is attested by the Mosaic law, Levit. XI, 21. 22., where four species of locust are permitted for eating: arbe, solam, chargol and chagab. So too the Talmudic doctors, who in the tractate Cholin, ch. 3, fol. 65 and 66, argue at length about the marks by which clean locusts are distinguished from unclean, that is, those which may be eaten from those whose eating is forbidden by the Law. Accordingly, at Exod. X, 19., where we read that a wind sent by God [III, 331] carried off whatever locusts were in Egypt and cast them into the Red Sea, so that not even one remained in all the borders of the Egyptians, Jonathan in his paraphrase makes an exception: מה דמלחין במנייא לצרוך מיכלהון, what they had preserved with salt in their vessels for use as food ^{(2)}.
